strengths: The paper addresses a relevant practical problem: improving the quality and speed of diffusion-based real-world super-resolution. The combination of a 16-channel latent space, task-adapted distillation, and simplified inference forms a coherent system.

Evaluation covers four synthetic and real-world benchmarks with relevant GAN, multistep diffusion, and one-step diffusion baselines. GenDR consistently achieves strong no-reference quality scores, including leading LIQE, MUSIQ, and Q-Align results.
Table 4 provides evidence that CiDA improves both OSEDiff and GenDR. The reported 77 ms inference time and qualitative examples suggest a promising perceptual-quality/latency trade-off.
weaknesses: The central CiD derivation is insufficiently justified. Replacing the generated latent with the paired HR latent in Eq. (8) changes the objective; it is not generally an identity transformation. No derivation establishes that the empirical combination in Eq. (9) yields the claimed unbiased optimization, particularly with approximate, jointly updated score networks and classifier-free guidance.

The evidence does not support broad claims of superior detail fidelity. On ImageNet-Test, GenDR's LPIPS is 0.2652 versus 0.2431 for OSEDiff and 0.2547 for InvSR. On RealSR, its PSNR is 23.18 dB versus 24.57 and 24.50 dB, respectively. Perceptual improvements can justify such trade-offs, but no-reference scores and attractive textures do not establish faithful recovery.

Ablations do not adequately isolate the contributions. The VAE4/VAE16 comparison also changes the pretrained backbone and training history, and lacks controlled full-reference reconstruction results. CiDA adds adversarial learning and representation alignment together, without separate ablations; real-score adaptation and the HR-latent substitution are also not isolated. Claimed training acceleration lacks convergence or compute measurements.

Human evaluation is inadequately documented: participant counts, evaluated image counts, sampling, randomization, instructions, and uncertainty are absent. This is especially consequential because human preference is used to support the larger latent space despite mixed objective results. DepictQA preferences cannot substitute for a reproducible human study or ground-truth fidelity evaluation.

Efficiency reporting needs a controlled protocol specifying resolution, hardware, precision, batch size, and timing boundaries. DreamClear uses three A100 GPUs, complicating the advertised speedup. The unqualified fastest/second-smallest claim also conflicts with Table 2: RealESRGAN is faster, while both GAN baselines and SinSR are smaller.

Reproducibility is limited by missing dataset selection and mixture details, degradation settings, the values of xi and the weighting constant C, precise gradient handling, and a complete training algorithm. The supplied manuscript refers to supplementary material that is not included.

Much of the system combines established SiD, REPA, adversarial distillation, LoRA, and an existing VAE. The potentially distinctive CiD modification therefore needs stronger technical justification and controlled evidence. The current experimental gains are promising, but unresolved soundness and evaluation issues place the submission below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses a relevant practical problem: improving the perceptual quality and speed of diffusion-based real-world super-resolution. Adapting an SD2.1-sized backbone to a 16-channel VAE is a potentially useful engineering contribution.

Reports consistent improvements on several perceptual metrics across four benchmarks, with relevant GAN, multistep diffusion, and one-step diffusion baselines. On RealLR200, MUSIQ improves from 69.03 for OSEDiff to 72.36.
The simplified pipeline achieves a reported 77 ms inference time versus 103 ms for OSEDiff and 115 ms for InvSR. Table 5 directly supports the efficiency benefit of caching fixed prompt embeddings.
Table 4 provides encouraging evidence for the combined distillation objective, including improvements when applied to OSEDiff. Qualitative examples and reported human preferences also favor GenDR.
weaknesses: The central CiD derivation is insufficiently justified. Replacing the generated latent with the paired HR latent in Equation (8) is described as an identity transformation, but minimizing their squared distance does not make them interchangeable during training. No derivation establishes that this substitution preserves the objective or gradient, and the claim that empirical weighting in Equation (9) ensures unbiased optimization is unsupported.

The evidence supports perceptual preference more convincingly than faithful reconstruction. In Table 2, GenDR has the lowest RealSR PSNR among all compared methods: 23.18 dB versus 24.57 for OSEDiff and 24.50 for InvSR. On ImageNet-Test, its LPIPS is worse than both methods. Such tradeoffs can be reasonable, but they undermine broad claims of superior detail fidelity without targeted tests distinguishing recovered details from plausible hallucinations.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed contributions adequately. The 4-channel versus 16-channel comparison also changes the pretrained backbone and its additional training, so it does not establish that latent dimensionality causes the gains. CiDA adds adversarial learning and representation alignment together, yet the text attributes the improvement to adversarial learning alone. Teacher adaptation and the HR-latent substitution are not separately evaluated, and training-acceleration claims lack convergence or wall-clock measurements.

Human evaluation is insufficiently documented despite its central role in supporting fidelity and the larger latent space. Participant counts, image counts, assignment and randomization procedures, uncertainty estimates, and significance tests are absent from the supplied manuscript. The reported 63.75% preference for VAE16 therefore cannot be assessed reliably.

Reproducibility and comparison fairness remain limited. The selected training corpus has no reported size or reproducible selection procedure, and includes additional FLUX-generated images. The supplied manuscript omits important settings such as the empirical coefficient ξ, CFG strength, and detailed gradient/update conventions. Baselines use official settings, but there is no matched-data or matched-training-budget comparison to separate methodological gains from additional pretraining.

Efficiency and novelty claims need tighter qualification. The reported 89.5× speedup compares against DreamClear running on three A100 GPUs, without a sufficiently specified common timing protocol. GenDR is the fastest listed diffusion method, but RealESRGAN is faster and several models are smaller. Most components build directly on existing SiD, DMD2, REPA, LoRA, and one-step SR techniques; the distinctive contribution could be meaningful, but its current theoretical justification and controlled experimental support are insufficient for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: improving the perceptual quality and inference speed of diffusion-based real-world super-resolution. The combination of a 16-channel latent representation and one-step restoration is well motivated.

Reported perceptual results are promising across four benchmarks. GenDR achieves the highest LIQE, MUSIQ, and Q-Align scores among the evaluated methods, with particularly consistent gains on RealLR200.

The simplified inference pipeline has practical value. Reported latency is 77 ms versus 103 ms for OSEDiff and 115 ms for InvSR, and Table 5 explicitly measures the overhead of alternative prompting strategies.

Comparisons include relevant GAN, multistep diffusion, and one-step diffusion baselines. Table 4 also shows improvements from CiDA when applied to OSEDiff, providing some evidence that the training approach transfers beyond the proposed backbone.
weaknesses: The central CiD derivation is insufficiently justified. Replacing the generated latent with the paired ground-truth latent in Eq. (8) generally changes the objective; being the optimum of a separate MSE loss does not establish an identity transformation. Likewise, the claim that the empirically weighted combination in Eq. (9) ensures unbiased optimization lacks a derivation or stated assumptions. This leaves the principal methodological claim unsupported.

The evidence supports improved perceptual quality more strongly than improved fidelity. On RealSR, GenDR has the lowest PSNR in Table 2: 23.18 dB versus 24.57 for OSEDiff and 24.50 for InvSR. On ImageNet-Test, its LPIPS is worse than both methods. These results do not invalidate perceptual SR, but they contradict broad claims of superior faithful restoration and require a clearer perception–distortion analysis.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed contributions adequately. The VAE4/VAE16 comparison also changes the pretrained backbone and training history, while GenDR uses additional selected and FLUX-generated training images. Table 4 combines adversarial learning and representation alignment into CiDA, so it cannot support attributing the remaining improvement specifically to adversarial learning. Separate teacher-adaptation, paired-target, adversarial, and REPA ablations are needed.

Human evaluation is not sufficiently documented: participant counts, image counts, sampling, presentation protocol, and uncertainty are absent. This is especially consequential because human preference is the main evidence favoring VAE16 when quantitative ablations are mixed. DepictQA preferences provide additional perceptual evidence but do not establish recovery of correct details.

Reproducibility remains incomplete in the supplied manuscript. Important details include the selected pretraining data and filtering procedure, the values of ξ and CFG strength, gradient-detachment conventions, and the precise alternating optimization procedure. Supplementary implementation details are referenced but are not included in the supplied PDF. The adversarial objective also needs an explicit optimization direction to resolve its positive log-likelihood sign within the combined loss.

Efficiency and training-acceleration claims need stronger controls. Timing resolution, precision, and measurement protocol are unspecified, and DreamClear uses three A100 GPUs. The added backbone training is substantial, but training cost and convergence curves are not reported. Overall, the promising empirical system does not yet overcome the unresolved derivation, attribution, and evaluation weaknesses sufficiently for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: GenDR addresses a practically relevant problem: improving the quality–latency trade-off of diffusion-based super-resolution. Combining a compact UNet with a 16-channel VAE is a useful architectural direction.

The reported efficiency is competitive: 77 ms versus 103 ms for OSEDiff and 115 ms for InvSR at the stated 512×512 setting. Cached prompt embeddings and shared score-network weights provide concrete engineering benefits.

Table 1 demonstrates consistent improvements in several no-reference quality metrics across synthetic and real benchmarks, particularly LIQE, MUSIQ, and Q-Align. Qualitative examples also show sharper, more visually convincing details.
The evaluation includes multiple established baselines, distillation and prompt ablations, VAE reconstruction comparisons, and deployment measurements across hardware and numerical precisions.
weaknesses: The central CiD justification is not established. Appendix A.1 assumes the current generator output equals an optimal conditional expectation given the noisy latent, although the actual generator receives the LR latent and need not attain that optimum. The noisy latent also depends on the generator parameters. An identity at an assumed optimum does not establish equality of training gradients away from it, and the empirical subtraction coefficient in Eq. (9) does not demonstrate the claimed unbiased optimization.

The adversarial training equations contain consequential sign inconsistencies. Algorithm 2 explicitly minimizes log D(real) + log(1 − D(fake)) for the discriminator and positively weighted log D(fake) for the generator, reversing the usual intended objectives. These may be transcription errors, but the published algorithm does not faithfully specify a working adversarial procedure.

Claims of superior fidelity exceed the evidence. On ImageNet-Test, GenDR has worse PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS than OSEDiff; on RealSR its PSNR is 23.18 dB versus 24.57 dB for OSEDiff and 24.50 dB for InvSR. Table 8 also shows that adding adversarial training improves no-reference scores while degrading LPIPS and PSNR. These results support a perceptual trade-off, not uniformly more faithful restoration.

The human evaluation is too limited to resolve the fidelity concern: it uses only 10 images, does not report participant counts or uncertainty, and Figure 6 shows SR–LR alignment preferences near chance against several competitors. Automated quality judges provide additional perceptual evidence but cannot establish recovery of correct missing details.

The ablations do not sufficiently isolate the proposed mechanisms. CiD simultaneously adapts the real score network and changes the target, without separate tests of those changes. The VAE comparison also changes pretrained models and training histories; under VSD, VAE16 actually reduces several no-reference scores relative to VAE4. Better autoencoder reconstruction and t-SNE visualizations do not establish that latent dimensionality causes the claimed downstream advantages. Quantitative comparisons with the discussed TVT and HYPIR approaches are also missing.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite substantial implementation detail. Dataset filtering retains 19.2% of images without specifying reproducible selection criteria, adaptation of the pretrained UNet's input/output channels is insufficiently described, and Algorithm 2 samples generator timesteps despite the fixed timestep stated in the main text. Table 8's description of retained reconstruction losses is also difficult to reconcile with the stated second-stage objective. These ambiguities matter given the substantial retraining budget.

strengths: GenDR addresses a practically relevant problem: improving the quality–latency trade-off in generative super-resolution. The reported 77 ms inference time versus 103 ms for OSEDiff and 115 ms for InvSR is a useful improvement.

The evaluation includes established GAN, multistep diffusion, and one-step diffusion baselines. GenDR consistently improves several no-reference quality metrics across synthetic and real-world benchmarks, with visually compelling examples.

The appendix provides substantive loss ablations, VAE reconstruction comparisons, and training/deployment measurements. Table 8 supports an empirical benefit from CiD over SiD, while Table 5 supports the reconstruction advantages of the selected 16-channel VAE.
weaknesses: The central CiD identity is not established for the actual training procedure. Appendix A.1 assumes the generator equals an optimal conditional mean given z_t, whereas the implemented generator takes z_l and z_t is subsequently constructed from its output. The proof therefore changes the conditioning problem and assumes an optimum that does not hold during training. It also does not establish gradient equivalence for the parameter-dependent sampling distribution or justify the claimed unbiased optimization with empirical weighting ξ.

Claims of superior fidelity and broad dominance exceed the evidence. In Table 1, GenDR's RealSR PSNR is 23.18 dB versus 24.57 for OSEDiff and 24.50 for InvSR. On ImageNet-Test, its LPIPS is 0.2652 versus 0.2431 and 0.2547, respectively. Table 8 also shows that adding adversarial learning to CiD worsens RealSR PSNR from 24.65 to 22.62 and LPIPS from 0.2527 to 0.2899. These results establish a perceptual-quality trade-off rather than consistently better faithful reconstruction.

The causal evidence for latent dimensionality is incomplete. The VAE4/VAE16 comparison changes the pretrained autoencoder and introduces substantial additional diffusion-model training without a clearly matched VAE4 retraining control. Under VSD, VAE16 actually lowers several metrics in Table 2. Likewise, the increase in T2I FID from 13.45 to 27.89 cannot establish that four-channel latents are inherently preferable; adaptation quality and training resources are confounded.

The human study uses only 10 images and does not report participant count, presentation randomization, uncertainty, or significance. Its comparison-method descriptions are inconsistent across sections. MLLM preferences provide supplementary evidence but cannot resolve whether generated details match the unknown high-resolution scene.

Important attribution and positioning gaps remain. CiD simultaneously adapts the real score network and replaces the generated target with the paired HR target, but these changes are not independently ablated. The cited TVT approach is directly relevant to the VAE contribution yet lacks a quantitative comparison; HYPIR appears only in a limited qualitative appendix comparison.

Reproducibility is weakened by unspecified image-filtering metrics and thresholds, dataset composition, and degradation-mixture details. The fixed generator timestep in the main text conflicts with sampled generator timesteps in Algorithm 2, and Table 7's RealSR results do not clearly reconcile with Table 1. These ambiguities matter given the substantial additional training budget.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical problem: improving the quality–latency trade-off in diffusion-based real-world super-resolution. Combining a compact UNet with a 16-channel VAE is a useful engineering direction.

Reported inference efficiency is compelling: GenDR takes 77 ms versus 103 ms for OSEDiff and 115 ms for InvSR. Additional deployment measurements across GPUs and numerical precisions strengthen the practical contribution.

Evaluation covers synthetic and real-world datasets, numerous established baselines, and diverse quality metrics. GenDR consistently achieves strong no-reference scores, including the best reported LIQE, MUSIQ, and Q-Align across the three main benchmarks.

The paper includes meaningful component ablations, training-cost measurements, and qualitative examples showing sharper, more plausible details. Table 2 supports benefits from CiDA with both VAE4 and VAE16.
weaknesses: The central CiD derivation is not established. Appendix A.1 assumes that the generated latent equals E[zh|zt], although the actual generator takes zl and zt is subsequently constructed by noising its output. MSE pretraining does not establish this conditional-expectation identity during distillation. Moreover, equality at an assumed optimum would not establish equality of training gradients away from that optimum. Consequently, replacing zg with zh in Equation (8), and claiming unbiased optimization through an empirical coefficient in Equation (9), lack adequate justification.

The adversarial optimization is incorrect as written. Algorithm 2 minimizes log D(real) + log(1−D(fake)) for the discriminator and minimizes a positive log D(fake) term for the generator. These directions reverse the intended GAN objectives. This may be a sign error in presentation, but it affects a central component and leaves the implemented training procedure uncertain.

The claim of superior fidelity is substantially stronger than the evidence. On ImageNet-Test, GenDR has worse PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS than OSEDiff. On RealSR, PSNR drops from 24.57 to 23.18 dB while LPIPS improves modestly. Table 8 likewise shows that adding adversarial training improves no-reference scores while worsening PSNR and LPIPS. These results support a perceptual trade-off, rather than generally more faithful restoration.

The subjective evaluation is insufficient to resolve this fidelity concern. It uses only 10 images, does not report participant counts or uncertainty, and inconsistently describes the comparator set. Preference for visual quality and alignment with an LR input cannot establish that generated high-frequency details are correct; automated MLLM preferences do not replace adequately powered human evaluation.

Ablations do not isolate several central claims. CiD combines real-score adaptation with the proposed target substitution without separating their effects. The VAE comparison also changes pretrained representations and training, and primarily reports no-reference SR metrics. Controlled fidelity comparisons and training-budget-matched experiments are needed. Closely related TVT is discussed without a quantitative comparison, while HYPIR appears only in supplementary qualitative examples.

Reproducibility remains limited despite the pseudocode: dataset filtering retains 19.2% of source images without specifying reproducible selection thresholds or the resulting dataset size, and training descriptions disagree on fixed versus sampled generator timesteps and training duration. Together with the unresolved objective definitions, these omissions make independent verification difficult.
